title: Thymus Embryology and the Adult Thymus
subject: Immune System (IMMU)
author: Dr. Sharilyn Rennie

overview.intro: This chapter follows the thymus from its origin in the third pharyngeal pouch, through colonization by blood-borne T cell precursors and the formation of cortex and medulla, to its descent into the mediastinum and its slow involution in adult life. It then applies that development to 22q11.2 deletion (DiGeorge) syndrome and to the anterior mediastinal masses. Board questions usually give a newborn with hypocalcemia, infections, and a heart defect, or an adult with a mediastinal mass, and ask you to name the failed structure or the likely tissue of origin. If you keep the three sources of the thymus separate (endoderm, neural crest, and marrow precursors), most of these questions follow directly.

connections.how: The cortical and medullary epithelium described here is the stroma that performs positive and negative selection.
Thymic aplasia and severe combined immunodeficiency both lower T cell counts, one from missing stroma and the other from defective precursors.
Parathyroid hypoplasia in DiGeorge syndrome produces the low PTH, low calcium, high phosphate pattern of hypoparathyroidism.
Cardiac neural crest cells that septate the outflow tract depend on the same pharyngeal field, explaining conotruncal defects in 22q11.2 deletion.
Thymoma and thymic follicular hyperplasia are linked to autoantibodies against the acetylcholine receptor in myasthenia gravis.

terms.def: An endodermal outpocketing of the embryonic foregut between two pharyngeal arches that gives rise to glands and cavities of the head, neck, and mediastinum.
An endoderm-derived stromal cell of the thymus, also called an epithelial reticular cell, that forms a meshwork and supplies the signals and self antigens that guide T cell maturation.
A developing T lymphocyte within the thymus.
A transcription factor required for thymic epithelial cell differentiation; its loss causes athymia with hair and nail defects.
A concentric whorl of flattened, keratinizing medullary epithelial cells that identifies thymic medulla on histology.
Autoimmune regulator, a protein in medullary thymic epithelial cells that switches on tissue-restricted self antigens so autoreactive thymocytes can be deleted.
A transcription factor gene within the 22q11.2 region whose haploinsufficiency disrupts development of the pharyngeal apparatus and outflow tract.
A congenital malformation of the cardiac outflow tract, such as truncus arteriosus, tetralogy of Fallot, or interrupted aortic arch.
The progressive, age-related loss of the T cell producing epithelial space of the thymus with replacement by adipose tissue.
Slow division of peripheral T cells driven by IL-7 or IL-15 and self peptide-MHC that maintains T cell numbers without antigen exposure.
A circular DNA fragment left after T cell receptor gene rearrangement that marks recently produced thymic emigrants because it is not copied when cells divide.
A neoplasm of thymic epithelial cells, usually in adults, associated with myasthenia gravis and other autoimmune disorders.

sections.title: Origin of the thymus and its descent into the mediastinum

blocks.text: The thymus is assembled from three sources. Endoderm of the third pharyngeal pouch forms the epithelial framework, neural crest derived mesenchyme forms the connective tissue, and blood-borne precursors later supply the lymphocytes (C02). Each source can fail on its own, so keeping them separate explains most embryology questions about this organ.

The pharyngeal apparatus consists of arches of mesoderm and neural crest mesenchyme, separated on the outside by ectodermal clefts and on the inside by endodermal pouches. Around the fifth to sixth week the third pouch forms a dorsal wing and a ventral wing. The dorsal wing becomes the inferior parathyroid gland, and the ventral wing becomes the thymus, so these two organs share an origin. The fourth pouch forms the superior parathyroids, and its ventral part, the ultimobranchial body, contributes the parafollicular (C) cells of the thyroid. Differentiation of the thymic epithelium depends on the transcription factor FOXN1. Loss of FOXN1 leaves a rudimentary thymus with no T cells, together with alopecia and nail dystrophy, which is the human counterpart of the nude mouse.

blocks.title: Pharyngeal pouch derivatives
rows: Middle ear cavity, pharyngotympanic (auditory) tube, mastoid antrum
Epithelial lining of the palatine tonsil and its crypts
Thymus (ventral wing) and inferior parathyroids (dorsal wing)
Superior parathyroids; ultimobranchial body (parafollicular C cells of the thyroid)
blocks.caption: The third pouch is the only pouch that gives rise to both an immune organ and an endocrine gland, which is why a single developmental defect can cause both T cell deficiency and hypocalcemia.

blocks.text: Cranial neural crest cells migrate into the pharyngeal arches and surround the thymic primordium. They form the capsule, the septa that divide the gland into incompletely separated lobules, and the connective tissue and pericytes around vessels entering the gland. This mesenchyme is not inert packing: its signals support growth of the epithelium, so a neural crest defect can leave the thymus small even when the endoderm is normal.

By about the seventh week the thymic primordia lose their connection with the pharynx and migrate caudally and medially. The left and right primordia meet in the midline and join loosely by connective tissue, which is why the gland remains bilobed rather than truly fused. They come to rest in the superior and anterior mediastinum, in front of the great vessels and pericardium. The inferior parathyroids travel with the thymus until they detach near the lower poles of the thyroid, ending below the fourth pouch glands. The pouch numbers therefore run opposite to the final positions of the parathyroids.

blocks.caption: Descent of the thymus drags the inferior parathyroids below the fourth pouch parathyroids.

blocks.text: Incomplete or excessive migration explains ectopic tissue. Thymic remnants can persist anywhere along the path from the angle of the mandible to the mediastinum, and cervical thymic cysts arise along the same line. An inferior parathyroid that fails to separate can be carried into the anterior mediastinum within the thymus, so a parathyroid adenoma causing hyperparathyroidism that is not found in the neck is often located along this third pouch route.

sections.title: Colonization by T cell precursors and formation of cortex and medulla

blocks.text: The endoderm builds a stromal framework but makes no lymphocytes. Thymic epithelial cells remain joined by desmosomes, as all epithelia are, yet they spread into a three-dimensional meshwork whose spaces fill with developing T cells (thymocytes). This stroma supplies what thymocytes cannot make for themselves: Notch ligands (delta-like 4) that commit precursors to the T lineage, interleukin 7 (IL-7) for survival and proliferation, chemokines that guide migration, and self peptides on MHC class I and II molecules for selection.

Hematopoietic progenitors begin entering the epithelial thymus at around the eighth to ninth week, attracted by chemokines such as CCL21 and CCL25. They come first from fetal liver and later from bone marrow. Because the lymphocytes are immigrants and the stroma is local, T cell deficiency can arise from either side: thymic aplasia removes the stroma, while severe combined immunodeficiency supplies precursors that cannot mature.

Once colonized, each lobule separates into a dense outer cortex and a paler inner medulla by about the end of the first trimester. Precursors enter through postcapillary venules near the corticomedullary junction, move outward to the subcapsular cortex while they proliferate, and then move inward as they mature. The cortex is crowded with small immature thymocytes, most CD4 and CD8 double positive, so it stains darkly. Cortical epithelial cells positively select thymocytes whose receptors can bind self peptide-MHC; most fail, die by apoptosis, and are cleared by macrophages. In the medulla, epithelial cells express AIRE, which switches on tissue-restricted antigens such as insulin, so strongly self-reactive thymocytes are deleted or diverted into regulatory T cells.

blocks.title: Cortex and medulla compared
rows: Immature, mostly CD4 and CD8 double positive
Mature CD4 or CD8 single positive
Positive selection by cortical epithelial cells
Negative selection by AIRE-expressing medullary epithelium and dendritic cells
blocks.caption: The thymus has lobules with cortex and medulla but, unlike a lymph node, no afferent lymphatics and no lymphoid follicles in the normal state.

blocks.text: Hassall corpuscles are concentric whorls of flattened, keratinizing medullary epithelial cells. They appear during fetal life, enlarge with age, and are the most reliable sign that tissue is thymus and the field is medulla. They secrete thymic stromal lymphopoietin, which conditions medullary dendritic cells to support regulatory T cell development. In the cortex, a blood-thymus barrier (continuous endothelium, thick basal lamina, an epithelial sheath, and perivascular macrophages) limits contact between circulating antigen and thymocytes during positive selection.

Survivors move inward to the medulla
AIRE-driven antigens delete strongly self-reactive cells
Naive single positive T cells exit to the blood
blocks.caption: Outward then inward migration places positive selection in the cortex and negative selection in the medulla.

blocks.predict: A fetus has normal bone marrow but lacks functional FOXN1. Would a cortex and medulla form, and would B cells be present?
blocks.explain: No cortex or medulla forms, because undifferentiated epithelium cannot attract precursors, supply Notch ligand and IL-7, or present self antigen. T cells are absent, while B cells, which mature in marrow, are present.

blocks.text: The 22q11.2 deletion syndrome is the most common human microdeletion syndrome, about 1 in 4,000 live births. A deletion of about 3 megabases on one chromosome 22 removes several dozen genes; most cases arise new, and transmission is autosomal dominant. DiGeorge and velocardiofacial syndrome are older names for the same deletion.

The key gene is TBX1, a transcription factor of pharyngeal endoderm and mesoderm. With one working copy, the pouches and arches segment poorly and fail to signal neural crest cells into the third and fourth arches and the outflow tract, so one deletion damages several neighboring structures that form at the same time.

blocks.title: From deletion to clinical findings
steps: 22q11.2 microdeletion removes TBX1 and neighboring genes
Pharyngeal pouches and arches segment poorly
Third and fourth pouch derivatives are hypoplastic
Neural crest fails to septate the outflow tract
Low T cells, low PTH, and conotruncal heart defects
blocks.caption: One field defect explains the immune, endocrine, and cardiac findings together.

blocks.text: Thymic hypoplasia is usual; true athymia (complete DiGeorge syndrome) occurs in under about 1% of cases. Few naive T cells are made, so CD3 positive counts are low while B cells and natural killer cells are normal. Infections follow the T cell pattern: viruses, Candida, and Pneumocystis jirovecii. Immunoglobulin levels are usually normal, though responses to protein antigens can be weak without T cell help. The broad anterior mediastinal shadow of the normal newborn thymus is absent on chest radiograph, but this sign is nonspecific, because severe combined immunodeficiency and stress involution in a sick neonate (C04) also shrink it.

Hypoplastic parathyroids secrete too little parathyroid hormone (PTH). Without PTH the distal tubule reabsorbs less calcium, the proximal tubule excretes less phosphate, bone releases less calcium, and renal 1-alpha-hydroxylase makes less calcitriol, reducing intestinal calcium absorption. The result is low calcium, high phosphate, and inappropriately low PTH. Low extracellular calcium lowers the threshold of nerve Na+ channels, so axons fire spontaneously: jitteriness, tetany, laryngospasm, and seizures in the first days of life. Adult total calcium is about 8.5 to 10.5 mg/dL (2.1 to 2.6 mmol/L), ionized about 1.1 to 1.3 mmol/L; neonatal values run slightly lower.

blocks.title: Failed structure and resulting finding
rows: Third pouch endoderm with neural crest
Low T cells, absent thymic shadow, viral, fungal, and Pneumocystis infections
Low PTH, hypocalcemia, hyperphosphatemia, tetany, seizures
Interrupted aortic arch type B, truncus arteriosus, tetralogy of Fallot, ventricular septal defect
Cleft palate or velopharyngeal insufficiency, characteristic facies
blocks.caption: Learning difficulties and later psychiatric illness, including schizophrenia, are also more common.

blocks.text: Cardiac neural crest cells form the aorticopulmonary septum. Too few cells leave septation absent or misaligned (truncus arteriosus, tetralogy of Fallot), and abnormal remodeling of the arch arteries gives interrupted aortic arch type B, the defect most specific for this deletion. Reduced thymic output also weakens central tolerance and regulatory T cell production, raising autoimmunity.

blocks.title: Worked example: a seizing newborn
blocks.text: A 3-day-old has a seizure. Total calcium is 6.4 mg/dL, phosphate is high, and PTH is low-normal. Echocardiography shows truncus arteriosus, and the chest radiograph shows no thymic shadow. Step 1: low calcium with high phosphate and an unraised PTH means parathyroid failure; vitamin D deficiency would raise PTH and lower phosphate. Step 2: a conotruncal defect points to failed cardiac neural crest. Step 3: an absent thymic shadow points to third pouch failure. One field defect links all three, so 22q11.2 deletion is the best explanation, and a low T cell count with normal B cells is the expected next finding.

sections.title: Thymic involution and persistence of peripheral T cell immunity

blocks.text: The thymus is largest relative to body weight at birth and largest in absolute size around puberty. Involution is the progressive loss of the true thymic epithelial space, the cortex and medulla where T cells are made. It begins in early childhood, well before puberty, and continues more slowly through adult life. Adipocytes accumulate between the lobules, so total gland size changes less than function: by late adulthood most of the thymus is fat surrounding small islands of cortex and medulla that still export a few naive T cells. The cortex thins first, the corticomedullary boundary blurs, and Hassall corpuscles remain prominent.

Several mechanisms contribute. Thymic epithelial cells express less FOXN1, sex steroids rising at puberty act on the epithelium and speed its loss, and aging marrow supplies fewer early progenitors. Acute involution is different and reversible. During severe illness, stress, or glucocorticoid exposure, double positive cortical thymocytes, which are highly sensitive to glucocorticoid-induced apoptosis, die in large numbers, and the gland can shrink within days. When the stress ends, for example after chemotherapy, the thymus can regrow beyond its earlier size, called thymic rebound, which can mimic a recurrent mediastinal mass on imaging.

Established T cell immunity survives involution because peripheral T cells are long-lived and maintain their own numbers. Naive T cells survive for years, sustained by IL-7 and by weak tonic T cell receptor signals from self peptide-MHC in lymph nodes. Memory T cells persist through slow turnover driven by IL-7 and IL-15. When numbers fall, each remaining cell receives more of these limited signals and divides, a process called homeostatic proliferation. In adults most new naive T cells come from this division of existing cells rather than from the thymus.

blocks.title: Homeostatic maintenance of the peripheral T cell pool
steps: Peripheral T cell numbers fall
Less IL-7 consumed, so more IL-7 per cell
IL-7 plus self peptide-MHC drives slow division
Pool size recovers toward its set point
More cells consume IL-7, slowing division
blocks.caption: Competition for IL-7 (and IL-15 for memory cells) holds T cell numbers steady with little thymic output.

blocks.text: For this reason thymectomy in an adult, for example to remove a thymoma, does not cause the clinical immunodeficiency seen in congenital athymia. The cost is subtle. The naive repertoire cannot be refilled with new receptor specificities, so after profound T cell loss from chemotherapy, HIV infection, or stem cell transplantation, adults recover slowly and mostly by expanding survivors, which narrows diversity. Recent thymic output can be estimated with T cell receptor excision circles (TRECs), DNA circles cut out during receptor gene rearrangement that are not copied when cells divide, so they dilute with homeostatic proliferation. Low TRECs on newborn screening flag severe combined immunodeficiency and athymia.

blocks.predict: Why does a 50-year-old who has her thymus removed keep normal T cell immunity, while an infant born without a thymus does not?
blocks.explain: The adult already has a large, diverse, self-renewing pool of naive and memory T cells maintained by IL-7, IL-15, and self peptide-MHC. The infant never built that pool, because the thymus is the only site where precursors become T cells.

sections.title: The adult thymus in the mediastinum and anterior mediastinal masses

blocks.text: In the anatomical scheme, a plane from the sternal angle to the T4 to T5 disc separates the superior from the inferior mediastinum, and the pericardium divides the inferior part into anterior, middle, and posterior compartments. The adult thymus lies mainly in the superior mediastinum behind the manubrium and extends into the anterior mediastinum between the sternum and pericardium, in front of the left brachiocephalic vein, superior vena cava, aortic arch, and upper pericardium. In children it is relatively larger and can reach toward the thyroid. Arteries come mainly from the internal thoracic arteries and veins drain mainly to the left brachiocephalic vein. Radiologists call this the prevascular compartment.

Masses here come from tissue that lives in or passes through the space: thymic epithelium, lymph nodes, germ cells, and thyroid extending from the neck. Age, associated findings, and contents on imaging sort them.

blocks.title: Classic anterior mediastinal masses
rows: Myasthenia gravis, pure red cell aplasia, hypogammaglobulinemia (Good syndrome)
Teratoma and other germ cell tumors
Fat, fluid, calcification, or teeth in teratoma; raised AFP or hCG in malignant germ cell tumors
Lymphocytes of mediastinal nodes or thymus
Young adult (nodular sclerosis Hodgkin, primary mediastinal large B cell); adolescent (T lymphoblastic)
Fever, night sweats, weight loss; other enlarged nodes; rapid growth
Mass continuous with a cervical goiter, tracheal deviation
blocks.caption: Often remembered as the four Ts: thymoma, teratoma, lymphoma, and thyroid.

blocks.text: Thymoma is a neoplasm of thymic epithelial cells, usually mixed with nonneoplastic immature T cells, and the most common primary anterior mediastinal tumor in adults. Many are encapsulated and slow growing, and capsular invasion largely determines behavior; thymic carcinoma is a separate, aggressive tumor. About 30 to 50% of patients with thymoma have myasthenia gravis, and about 10 to 15% of patients with myasthenia have a thymoma. The neoplastic epithelium often lacks AIRE, so it selects T cells but fails to delete autoreactive ones, which help B cells make antibodies against the acetylcholine receptor; similar autoimmunity underlies pure red cell aplasia, while the cause of hypogammaglobulinemia with few B cells (Good syndrome) is unclear. Thymic follicular hyperplasia, germinal centers in the medulla of most younger patients with antibody positive myasthenia, is not a tumor.

Any large anterior mass can compress its neighbors: the superior vena cava (facial and arm swelling, distended neck veins), the trachea (stridor, worse lying flat), and the phrenic nerve (raised hemidiaphragm). Fast-growing tumors such as T lymphoblastic lymphoma produce these effects over days to weeks.

blocks.title: Worked example: sorting two anterior mediastinal masses
blocks.text: Patient A, 55, has drooping eyelids and double vision that worsen through the day, and a smooth anterior mediastinal soft tissue mass without fat or calcium. Fatigable weakness indicates acetylcholine receptor antibodies, and an adult with this autoimmunity and a thymic mass most likely has a thymoma. Patient B, 20, has a mass containing fat and calcification with a normal AFP: age and contents indicate a mature teratoma. A high AFP would instead indicate a yolk sac component of a malignant nonseminomatous germ cell tumor, because thymic epithelium and lymphocytes do not make AFP.

blocks.predict: A 23-year-old woman has a large anterior mediastinal mass, night sweats, and an enlarged supraclavicular node. Which mass is most likely, and why is thymoma less likely?
blocks.explain: Lymphoma, most likely nodular sclerosis Hodgkin: B symptoms and nodal spread reflect a lymphocyte tumor. Thymoma is an epithelial tumor of older adults that presents with autoimmunity or mass effect, not B symptoms.

integration.text: Embryology and anatomy explain the pattern of disease. The third pharyngeal pouch makes both the thymus and the inferior parathyroids, and neural crest cells from the same pharyngeal region septate the cardiac outflow tract, so one field defect in 22q11.2 deletion produces T cell deficiency, hypocalcemia, and conotruncal heart disease together. The descent of the thymus explains ectopic parathyroid and thymic tissue in the neck and mediastinum, and its final position behind the manubrium, in front of the great veins, explains why its masses compress the superior vena cava and trachea.

Immunology and pathology connect structure to function. The epithelium of the cortex and medulla selects T cells, so an absent thymus causes immunodeficiency, while a neoplastic thymus that selects badly causes autoimmunity such as myasthenia gravis. Once the peripheral pool is built, IL-7 and IL-15 driven homeostatic proliferation sustains it, so involution and adult thymectomy cost repertoire diversity rather than causing overt immunodeficiency. Limits remain: the chest radiograph shadow is nonspecific in sick neonates, and the residual function of the adult thymus varies widely between individuals.

summary: The thymic epithelium comes from ventral third pouch endoderm, the capsule and septa from neural crest, and the lymphocytes from fetal liver and bone marrow precursors.
The third pouch also forms the inferior parathyroids, which the descending thymus pulls below the fourth pouch superior parathyroids.
Thymic epithelium supplies Notch ligand, IL-7, chemokines, and self peptide-MHC; FOXN1 loss leaves no functional thymus.
The dark cortex holds immature double positive thymocytes and performs positive selection; the pale medulla holds AIRE-expressing epithelium, Hassall corpuscles, and performs negative selection.
22q11.2 deletion (TBX1 haploinsufficiency) causes thymic hypoplasia with low T cells and normal B cells, hypoparathyroid hypocalcemia with high phosphate, and conotruncal defects.
Involution replaces the thymic epithelial space with fat from childhood onward; glucocorticoids cause acute, reversible loss of cortical thymocytes.
Peripheral T cells persist after involution or adult thymectomy through IL-7 and IL-15 driven homeostatic proliferation; TRECs measure recent thymic output.
The adult thymus lies in the superior and anterior mediastinum behind the manubrium, in front of the left brachiocephalic vein and great vessels.
Anterior mediastinal masses are thymoma, teratoma and other germ cell tumors, lymphoma, and retrosternal thyroid, sorted by age, contents, and associated findings.
Thymoma is an epithelial tumor of older adults associated with myasthenia gravis and pure red cell aplasia through defective tolerance, and with hypogammaglobulinemia.

verify: Timing of pouch events (third pouch wings at about weeks 5 to 6, detachment at about week 7, lymphoid colonization at about weeks 8 to 9, cortex and medulla by the end of the first trimester) varies slightly between embryology texts; values are given as approximate.

Some sources propose an ectodermal (third cleft) contribution to the thymic cortex; this chapter follows the current consensus that thymic epithelium is entirely third pouch endoderm. Confirm NABNE does not test the older view.
The incidence of 22q11.2 deletion is quoted from about 1 in 3,000 to 1 in 6,000 live births; this chapter uses about 1 in 4,000.
Proportions for complete DiGeorge (under about 1%), myasthenia gravis in thymoma (about 30 to 50%), and thymoma in myasthenia gravis (about 10 to 15%) vary among series.
Thymic weight at puberty (often quoted as 30 to 40 g) varies between sources and was omitted.
Registry data link adult thymectomy to later cancer and autoimmunity; the mechanism of Good syndrome hypogammaglobulinemia is unsettled.
Confirm whether NABNE uses the anatomical four-part mediastinal division or the radiologic three-compartment (prevascular, visceral, paravertebral) scheme for mass questions.
Confirm the four Ts mnemonic is acceptable in course materials.

Requested new diagram names for a future revision: pharyngeal-pouches (pouch derivatives and parathyroid descent), thymus-lobule (cortex, medulla, Hassall corpuscles, thymocyte migration), and mediastinum-compartments (thymus position and anterior mass sites).
